title: The Westbrook Repair Café
context: You will hear the founder of a community repair café talking to people who are interested in volunteering.

lines.t: Hi everyone, and thanks for coming along to this information evening. I'm Joanne, and I set up the Westbrook Repair Café about four years ago. For anyone who hasn't been to one of our sessions, the idea is simple. Once a month, people bring in things that are broken, a toaster, a jacket with a torn zip, a wobbly chair, and our volunteers try to fix them, for free.

People often assume I started it for environmental reasons, and of course keeping things out of landfill matters a great deal. And yes, visitors do pick up a few repair skills along the way. But to be honest, the real reason was more personal. I'd just moved here and didn't know a soul, and I wanted a way for neighbours to get together and actually talk to each other.

Our first sessions were in the library, but we ran out of room very quickly. The community centre offered us a space, but only on weekday mornings, which didn't suit most people. So for the last two years we've been in the scout hall on Mill Road, and that works really well.

One question we get a lot is about spare parts. We don't keep a stock of parts, because there are simply too many different kinds. So if your item needs a new part, the volunteer will tell you exactly what to get, and you buy it yourself and bring it back to the next session. We never order parts for people, and volunteers don't handle any money.

What's our biggest challenge? Well, you might think it's finding volunteers, but we're actually very lucky there. And people very rarely bring anything unsafe. No, the real problem is the queues. Lots of visitors turn up the minute we open, and some of them end up waiting for two hours or more. We're still working on a solution to that.
Now, let me tell you a bit about each of our repair tables, so you can think about where you'd like to help.

The electrical table is where it all began. On our very first day it was the only table we had, just me and a retired electrician with a box of screwdrivers. People expect a long wait for electrical repairs, but in fact most jobs there take less than twenty minutes.

The bicycle table has always been squeezed into a corner of the main hall, and bikes take up a lot of space. So from next month it'll be moving out into the covered yard at the back of the building, where there's much more room.

At the clothing table, the volunteers don't just mend things for you. They'll sit you down at a sewing machine and show you how to do the repair yourself, so next time you won't need us. It's become one of our most popular tables.

The furniture table is a bit different. Because chairs and tables are so big and awkward to carry, we can only take furniture that has been booked in beforehand, through our website. Please don't turn up with a sofa on the day.
Then there's the jewellery table. It's run by a lovely volunteer called Pam, who has to leave at midday to look after her grandchildren, so that table finishes an hour before everything else.

And finally, the computer table. People bring in laptops and tablets, and demand has grown enormously. At the moment we only have one volunteer there, so if you know anything about computers, we'd love to hear from you, because we urgently need at least two more.
Right, if you'd like to sign up, there are forms on the table by the door. Let's have a short break and then I'll answer your questions.
